title: The globular cluster Omega Centauri
caption: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
celestial: NGC 5139, Omega Centauri · constellation Centaurus · about 17000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This ESO image looks into the central part of Omega Centauri, a globular cluster that holds as many as ten million stars. Even this central region covers a patch of sky about as big as the full Moon, roughly half a degree across.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical collection of stars bound together by gravity, and Omega Centauri, also known as NGC 5139, counts its stars in the millions. The picture was captured from ESO's La Silla Observatory with the Wide Field Imager, and it is a colour composite of images taken through three filters known as B, V and I.

There is a small puzzle hidden in the frame. The Wide Field Imager uses a mosaic of detectors, which leaves narrow gaps between them. Two small gaps in this image were patched with lower-quality data from the Digitized Sky Survey, and ESO invites viewers to try to spot them. North is at the top and east is to the left.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (31.88 x 29.99 arcminutes) and distance (17000 light years), the frame spans roughly 158 × 148 light-years. Its light set out about 17,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This colour composite from the Wide Field Imager combines images taken through B, V and I filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The I-band light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye, and long camera exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The cluster lies about 17,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Centaurus. Its alternative name, NGC 5139, is its number in the New General Catalogue, a long-standing list of nebulae, clusters and galaxies.
alt: The dense central part of the globular cluster Omega Centauri, packed with stars.
